chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter II
paragraphs: What force moves nations?

Biographical historians and historians of individual nations understand this force as a power inherent in heroes and rulers. In their accounts, events happen solely through the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whatever person they happen to be describing. The answers these historians give to the question of what force drives events are satisfying only as long as there is just one historian for each event. But as soon as historians of different nations and perspectives begin describing the same event, the answers they give immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each historian not only differently but often in completely opposite ways.

Writers of universal history who deal with all nations seem to recognize how flawed the specialist historians' view of this force is. They do not see it as a power inherent in heroes and rulers, but as the result of many different forces acting in various directions. In describing a war or the conquest of a people, the universal historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of any one person, but in the interaction of many persons connected with the event.

According to this view, the power of historical figures—represented as the product of many forces—can no longer be treated as a force that itself produces events. Yet in most cases, universal historians still use the concept of power as a force that independently produces events, treating it as both cause and effect at the same time.

This strange contradiction is not accidental. Not only does it crop up at every turn, but universal historians' accounts are entirely made up of such contradictions. This contradiction arises because, having entered the field of analysis, the universal historians stop halfway.

To find component forces equal to the combined or resultant force, the sum of the components must equal the result. This condition is never met by the universal historians, and so to explain the resultant forces they are forced to admit—in addition to the insufficient components—an unexplained force acting upon the result.

A specialist historian describing the campaign of 1813 or the restoration of the Bourbons plainly asserts that these events were produced by the will of Alexander. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view, tries to prove that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons were caused not only by Alexander but also by Stein, Metternich, Madame de Stael, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian has evidently broken down Alexander's power into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of these components—that is, the interaction of Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Stael, and the others—obviously does not equal the whole result. The fact that millions of Christian men killed one another and devastated Europe was clearly not caused only by these individuals' activity. And therefore, the universal historian—after having broken down Alexander's power into components and proved them insufficient—must again accept the unexplained force called "power" and recognize it as the influence of great men on events, which is precisely the same thing the specialist historian said.

Peasants who have no clear idea of the cause of rain say, depending on whether they want rain or sunshine: "The wind has blown the clouds away" or "The wind has brought the clouds." In exactly the same way, the universal historians sometimes—when it suits them and fits their theory—say that power is the result of events, and sometimes—when they need to prove something else—say that power produces events.

A third class of historians—the so-called cultural historians—following the path laid down by the universal historians who sometimes accept writers and ladies as forces that produce events—take this force to be something else entirely. They locate it in what is called culture—in intellectual activity.

The cultural historians are perfectly consistent with their predecessors, the universal historians. If historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in certain ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the vast number of indicators that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians select the indicator of intellectual activity and declare it to be the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, only with great reluctance can one agree that there is any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples—and it is quite impossible to admit that intellectual activity guides the actions of people, because phenomena like the brutal murders of the French Revolution, which resulted from preaching about human equality, do not support such a conclusion.

But even granting all the cleverly constructed arguments with which these histories are filled—granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an "idea"—history's essential question still remains unanswered. To the former power of monarchs and the influence of advisors and other individuals, a new force has now been added: the power of ideas. But how this new force is connected to events—that is, how one particular idea out of the millions of ideas that exist gives rise to a particular event—still needs to be explained.

Undoubtedly some relationship exists between all people who live at the same time, and so it is possible to find connections between the intellectual activity of people and their historical movements, just as connections can be found between the movements of humanity and trade, handicrafts, gardening, or anything else you care to name.

But to say nothing of the intrinsic quality of these cultural histories—which may perhaps be of some use to someone—they are significant because, after seriously and minutely examining various religious, philosophical, and political doctrines as causes of events, every time history has to describe an actual historical event—such as the campaign of 1812—they involuntarily describe it as the result of power, plainly stating that the campaign was the product of Napoleon's will. In saying this, the cultural historians inadvertently contradict themselves, proving that the new force they have invented does not explain events, and that the only way to understand history is through the very power they pretend to reject.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter III
paragraphs: A locomotive is moving. Someone asks: "What makes it move?" A peasant says the devil moves it. Another man says the locomotive moves because its wheels turn. A third insists the cause lies in the smoke the wind carries away.

The peasant is irrefutable. He has devised a complete explanation. To refute him, someone would have to prove there is no devil, or another peasant would have to explain that it's not the devil but a German who moves the locomotive. Only then, seeing the contradiction, would they both realize they were both wrong. But the man who says the cause is the turning of the wheels refutes himself, because having entered the realm of analysis, he would need to keep going: he must explain why the wheels turn, and until he arrives at the ultimate cause—the steam compressed in the boiler—he has no right to stop. The man who explains the movement by the smoke being carried away, noticing that the wheels don't provide a sufficient explanation, has seized on the first thing that catches his eye and, from the other side, offered that as an explanation.
The only concept that can explain the movement of the locomotive is one of a force proportionate to the movement observed.
The only concept that can explain the movement of peoples is one of a force proportionate to the entire movement of the peoples.

Yet to supply this concept, various historians invoke forces of different kinds, all disproportionate to the movement observed. Some see it as a force directly inherent in heroes, as the peasant sees the devil in the locomotive; others as a force resulting from several other forces, like the turning of the wheels; still others as an intellectual influence, like the smoke being blown away.

As long as histories are written about individual people—whether Caesars, Alexanders, Luthers, or Voltaires—and not about all the people, absolutely all those who take part in an event, it is impossible to describe the movement of humanity without the concept of a force that compels people to direct their activity toward a single end. And the only such concept known to historians is power.

This concept is the one handle by which the material of history, as currently understood, can be grasped. Anyone who breaks off that handle—as Buckle did—without finding another method of treating historical material, simply deprives himself of the only possible way of dealing with it. The inevitability of the concept of power to explain historical phenomena is best demonstrated by the universal historians and cultural historians themselves, who—despite ostensibly rejecting the concept of power—in fact use it at every step.

In dealing with humanity's inquiry, the science of history up to now is like money in circulation—paper money and coin. The biographies and national histories are like paper money. They can be used and can circulate and serve their purpose without harming anyone—and even usefully—as long as no one questions whether they're backed by anything real. You only need to forget to ask how the will of heroes produces events—and the histories of the Thiers type will be interesting, instructive, and may even have a touch of poetry. But just as doubts about the real value of paper money arise either because it's easy to print too much of it, or because people try to exchange it for gold—so too doubts about the real meaning of this kind of history arise either because too many such histories are written, or because someone naively asks: by what force did Napoleon do all this?—that is, tries to exchange the current paper money for the real gold of genuine understanding.

The writers of universal history and cultural history are like people who, recognizing the defects of paper money, decide to replace it with coins made of metal that lacks the specific gravity of gold. Their coins may jingle, but that's all. Paper money may deceive the ignorant, but nobody is deceived by base-metal coins that only jingle. Just as gold is gold only when it can be used not just for exchange but also in itself, so too universal history will be gold only when it can answer history's essential question: what is power? Universal historians answer this question contradictorily, and cultural historians sidestep it entirely, answering something completely different. And just as tokens resembling gold can only be used among a group of people who agree to accept them as gold, or among people who don't know the nature of gold, so too universal historians and cultural historians—who fail to answer the essential questions of humanity—serve as currency only in universities and among the mass of readers who have a taste for what they call "serious reading."

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Having abandoned the ancients' concept that the will of a nation is divinely subjected to one chosen man and that man's will is subjected to God, history cannot take a single step without contradiction until it chooses one of two things: either a return to the old belief in the direct intervention of God in human affairs, or a definite explanation of what is meant by the "power" that produces historical events.
A return to the first option is impossible—the belief has been destroyed. And so it is essential to explain what is meant by power.

Napoleon ordered an army to be raised and to march to war. We are so accustomed to this idea and have grown so used to it that the question—why did six hundred thousand men go fight when Napoleon said certain words?—seems absurd. He had the power, and so his orders were carried out.

This answer is perfectly satisfactory if we believe his power came from God. But as soon as we reject that belief, it becomes essential to determine what this power of one man over others actually is.

It cannot be the direct physical power of a strong man over a weak one—domination based on the application or threat of physical force, like the power of Hercules. Nor can it rest on moral force, as some simplistic historians think when they say that the leading figures in history are heroes, endowed with a special strength of soul and mind called genius. This power cannot be based on moral superiority, because—not to mention the fact that heroes like Napoleon whose moral qualities are hotly debated can hardly be held up as examples of moral superiority—history shows us that neither a Louis XI nor a Metternich, who governed millions, possessed any particular strength of soul, but on the contrary were generally morally weaker than any of the millions they governed.

If the source of power lies neither in the physical nor in the moral qualities of the person who possesses it, then it must evidently be found elsewhere—in the relationship between that person and the people.
And that is exactly how the science of jurisprudence understands power—jurisprudence being that exchange bank of history which offers to trade history's concept of power for real gold.
Power is the collective will of the people, transferred by expressed or tacit consent to their chosen rulers.

In the realm of jurisprudence—which consists of discussions about how a state and power might be arranged if it were possible to arrange them—this is all perfectly clear. But when applied to history, this definition of power needs explanation.

Jurisprudence regards the state and power as the ancients regarded fire—as something that exists absolutely. But for history, the state and power are merely phenomena, just as for modern physics, fire is not an element but a phenomenon.

From this fundamental difference between the historical and the legal view, it follows that jurisprudence can describe in detail how, in its opinion, power should be organized and what power—existing immutably outside of time—is. But to history's questions about the meaning of power as it constantly changes over time, jurisprudence can give no answer.

If power is the collective will of the people transferred to their ruler, was Pugachev a representative of the people's will? If not, why was Napoleon I? Why was Napoleon III a criminal when he was captured at Boulogne, and why were the people he later arrested the criminals?

Do palace coups—in which sometimes only two or three people are involved—transfer the will of the people to a new ruler? In international relations, is the will of the people also transferred to their conqueror? Was the will of the Rhine Confederation transferred to Napoleon in 1806? Was the will of the Russian people transferred to Napoleon in 1809, when our army marched with the French to fight Austria?
To these questions, three answers are possible:

Either we assume: (1) that the will of the people is always unconditionally transferred to the ruler or rulers they have chosen, and therefore every emergence of a new power, every struggle against the appointed power, must be regarded as a violation of the real power; or (2) that the will of the people is conditionally transferred to their rulers, on definite and known conditions, and we can show that all cases of restraint, opposition, and even destruction of power result from rulers failing to observe the conditions on which power was transferred to them; or (3) that the will of the people is conditionally transferred to their rulers, but on conditions that are undefined and unknown, and that the emergence of multiple authorities, their struggles and falls, result only from the greater or lesser fulfillment of those unknown conditions on which the will of the people is transferred from one set of persons to another.
And these are the three ways historians explain the relationship of peoples to their rulers.

Some historians—those biographical and specialist historians already mentioned—who in their simplicity fail to grasp the question of what power means, seem to assume that the collective will of the people is unconditionally transferred to historical figures, and therefore when describing any power they treat it as the one real, absolute, and inviolable power.

Their theory works well for primitive and peaceful periods of history, but has the disadvantage—when applied to complex and turbulent periods when various powers arise simultaneously and struggle with one another—that a Legitimist historian will prove that the National Convention, the Directory, and Bonaparte were nothing but violations of true power, while a Republican and a Bonapartist will prove the opposite: that the one they favor was the true power and that the others were violations of it. Obviously, these historians' mutual contradictions cancel each other out.

Recognizing the falseness of this view, another set of historians says that power rests on a conditional delegation of the people's will to their rulers, and that historical leaders have power only on the condition that they carry out the program which the people's will has, by tacit agreement, prescribed for them. But what this program consists of, these historians do not tell us—or if they do, they constantly contradict one another.

Each historian, according to his own idea of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for the key conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But not only do historians contradict each other about the nature of this program—even admitting that one such program exists for all nations—the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions on which power is delegated are a nation's wealth, freedom, or enlightenment, why did a Louis XIV or an Ivan the Terrible live out their reigns in peace, while a Louis XVI or a Charles I were executed by their peoples? To this question the historians have no answer. If the connection between rulers and peoples is based on conditions, then why should people who violate those conditions be punished—punished by execution or by disgrace—by the very people who put them in power on those conditions?

These historians are like a botanist who, noticing that some plants grow from seeds that produce two first leaves, insists that everything that grows does so by sprouting two leaves. The palm, the mushroom, and even the oak—which grow into full size and no longer resemble two leaves—these the botanist would have to say deviate from his theory.

Historians of the third class assume that the will of the people is transferred to historical figures conditionally, but that the conditions are unknown to us. They say historical figures have power only because they fulfill the will of the people which has been delegated to them.
But in that case, if the force that moves nations lies not in the leaders but in the nations themselves, what significance do those leaders have?
The leaders, these historians tell us, express the will of the people: the activity of the leaders represents the activity of the people.

But then the question arises: does all of the leaders' activity serve as an expression of the people's will, or only part of it? If all the leaders' activity represents the people's will, as some historians think, then all the details of court scandals in the Napoleonic biographies represent the life of the nation—which is obviously absurd. If only part of the historical leaders' activity represents the people's will, as other historians think, then to determine which part represents the people's will, we must first know what the people's will actually is.

Faced with this difficulty, historians of this class devise some extremely vague, intangible, and general abstraction that can cover every conceivable occurrence, and declare this abstraction to be the goal of humanity's movement. The most common such generalizations are: freedom, equality, enlightenment, progress, civilization, and culture. Having posited some such abstraction as the goal of humanity's movement, the historians study those individuals who have left the most memoirs behind them—kings, ministers, generals, writers, reformers, popes, and journalists—and to the extent that these individuals seem to have promoted or hindered that abstraction, call them great or small, good or bad. But since no one has ever proved that the goal of humanity is freedom, equality, enlightenment, or civilization—and since the connection between the masses and the rulers and enlighteners of humanity rests only on the arbitrary assumption that the collective will of the masses is always transferred to those figures whom we happen to notice—the activity of the millions of people who migrate, burn houses, abandon farming, and slaughter one another is never expressed in the description of the activity of some dozen people who did not burn houses, practice farming, or kill their fellow men.

History proves this at every step. Is the ferment of the peoples of the West at the end of the eighteenth century and their drive eastward explained by the activity of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, their mistresses and ministers, and the lives of Napoleon, Rousseau, Diderot, Beaumarchais, and others?
Is the movement of the Russian people eastward to Kazan and Siberia expressed by the details of Ivan the Terrible's disturbed character and his correspondence with Kurbsky?

Is the movement of the peoples during the Crusades explained by the lives and activity of the Godfreys and the Louises and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east—without leaders, with a crowd of vagabonds and Peter the Hermit—remains incomprehensible. And still more incomprehensible is the cessation of that movement just when a rational and sacred goal for the Crusades—the liberation of Jerusalem—had been clearly set by the historic leaders. Popes, kings, and knights encouraged people to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had previously driven them to move no longer existed.
Still less does the history of writers and reformers explain to us the life of peoples.

The history of culture tells us about the impulses and conditions that shaped a writer's or reformer's life and thought. We learn that Luther had a hot temper and said such-and-such things; we learn that Rousseau was suspicious and wrote such-and-such books. But we do not learn why, after the Reformation, people slaughtered one another, or why, during the French Revolution, they executed one another.
If we combine both these kinds of history, as the newest historians do, we get the history of monarchs and writers, but not the history of the life of peoples.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter V
paragraphs: The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a few men, because the connection between those men and the nations has not been found. The theory that this connection is based on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical persons is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historic persons may explain much in the domain of jurisprudence and may be essential for its purposes; but in its application to history—as soon as revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur, that is, as soon as history actually begins—the theory explains nothing.
The theory seems irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will can never be verified, since it never actually occurred.
Whatever happens and whoever stands at the head of affairs, the theory can always say that such-and-such a person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

The answers this theory gives to historical questions are like the replies of a man who, watching the movements of a herd of cattle and paying no attention to the varying quality of the pasture in different parts of the field, or to the herdsman's driving, attributes the herd's direction to whichever animal happens to be at the front.

"The herd goes in that direction because the animal in front leads it, and the collective will of all the other animals is vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say—those who assume the unconditional transfer of the people's will.

"If the animals at the front of the herd change, this happens because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction chosen by the whole herd." This is the answer given by historians who assume the collective will of the masses is transferred to rulers on certain conditions which they regard as known.

"If the animals at the front keep changing and the whole herd keeps shifting direction, this is because—in order to follow a given direction—the animals transfer their will to whichever animal has caught our attention, and so to study the movement of the herd we must observe all the noticeable animals moving on all sides of the herd." So say the third class of historians who consider all historical figures—from monarchs to journalists—as expressions of their time.
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical persons is merely a paraphrase—a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what conditions is the will of the people delegated to one person? On the condition that the person expresses the will of the whole people. That is, power is power. In other words: power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then—having critically examined the explanation of "power" that jurisprudence offers—humanity would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence. But for understanding phenomena, besides abstract reasoning, people have another instrument: experience. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word but an actually existing phenomenon.
Not to mention that no description of collective human activity can do without the concept of power, the existence of power is proved both by history and by observing present-day events.

Whenever an event occurs, a person or persons appear by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and Bismarck issue decrees and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree and an army enters Russia. Alexander I issues a decree and the French submit to the Bourbons. Experience shows us that whenever an event takes place it is connected with the will of one or several people who ordered it.

Historians, following their old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, try to see the cause of events in the expression of the will of someone endowed with power. But this assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a person's will—his words—are only part of the total activity expressed in an event, such as a war or a revolution. And so, without invoking some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words can be the immediate cause of the movement of millions of people.

On the other hand, even if we admitted that words can be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of historical figures' wills in most cases produces no effect at all—that is, their orders are often not carried out, and sometimes the very opposite of what they commanded takes place.
Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot regard "power" as the cause of events.
Power, from the standpoint of experience, is merely the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.
To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a concept of the expression of will, referring it to man and not to God.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Only the expression of God's will, which is independent of time, can relate to a whole series of events spanning years or centuries, and only God, independent of everything, can by His will alone determine the direction of humanity's movement. But a human being acts in time and is himself part of events.

Restoring the first condition that was left out—the element of time—we see that no command can be carried out unless some prior command has already been given that makes the execution of the latest one possible.

No command ever appears out of nowhere or covers an entire series of events by itself; each command follows from another, and each always relates to one specific moment of an event, never to a whole series.

When we say, for instance, that Napoleon ordered armies to go to war, we are combining in one simultaneous expression a whole series of consecutive commands that depended on one another. Napoleon could not have commanded an invasion of Russia and never did so. One day he ordered certain papers to be written to Vienna, to Berlin, and to Petersburg; the next day he ordered certain decrees and instructions to the army, the fleet, and the commissariat, and so on and so on—millions of commands making up a series of commands corresponding to a series of events that brought the French army to Russia.

If throughout his reign Napoleon issued commands about an invasion of England—spending more time and effort on that project than on any other—yet during his whole reign never once attempted it, and instead invaded Russia, with which he considered it advantageous to be allied, this was because the first set of commands did not and could not correspond to the course of events, while the second set did.

For an order to be reliably carried out, a person must command what can actually be done. But knowing what can and what cannot be done is impossible—not only in the case of Napoleon's invasion of Russia, where millions of people participated, but even in the simplest event—because in either case millions of obstacles may arise.

Our mistaken belief that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that, after the event has taken place, out of thousands of commands only those few that happened to match the event are remembered as having been carried out. We forget about the others because they didn't match the event and therefore weren't executed.

We say that Napoleon wanted to invade Russia and invaded it. In reality, throughout Napoleon's entire career we never find anything resembling an expression of that desire. What we find is a series of commands—expressions of his will—that are enormously varied and vaguely directed. Out of Napoleon's countless series of unexecuted orders, one series—for the campaign of 1812—was carried out, not because those particular orders differed in any way from the ones that weren't, but because they happened to coincide with the course of events that led the French army into Russia. Just as a stencil doesn't produce the image on a wall because paint was applied from this side or that, but because paint was applied from all sides of the stencil's cut-out shape.
So, examining the relationship between commands and events in time, we find that a command can never be the cause of an event, but that a definite interdependence exists between the two.

To understand what this interdependence consists of, it is necessary to restore another condition that was left out of every command—a condition that applies to commands issued by human beings, not by God: the person who gives the command is himself a participant in the event.
This relationship of the commander to those he commands is precisely what is called power. This relationship consists in the following:

For collective action, people always combine into certain groups, and in these groups—regardless of the differences in the goals set for the collective action—the relationship between participants is always the same.

People who unite in these groups always relate to one another in such a way that the greater number take a more direct part, and the smaller number take a less direct part, in the collective action they have joined together to perform.
Of all the groups in which people combine for collective action, one of the most clear-cut and well-defined examples is an army.

Every army is made up of the lowest ranks—the ordinary soldiers—of whom there are always the most; of the next higher rank—corporals and non-commissioned officers, of whom there are fewer; of still higher officers, of whom there are fewer yet; and so on up to the highest military command, which is concentrated in a single person.

A military organization can be precisely compared to a cone, whose base—the widest part—consists of the rank and file; the next section, narrower and higher, consists of the next grades of the army; and so on to the apex of the cone, which represents the commander-in-chief.

The soldiers, who are the most numerous, form the lowest section and the base of the cone. The ordinary soldier does the actual fighting—the stabbing, hacking, burning, and looting—and always receives his orders from those above him; he never gives orders himself. The non-commissioned officers (of whom there are fewer) less often perform the actual fighting than the soldiers, but they do give orders. An officer still more rarely takes direct part in the action, and gives orders more frequently. A general does nothing but command troops, indicate the objective, and hardly ever uses a weapon himself. The commander-in-chief never takes direct part in the action at all, and only makes general plans for the movement of the masses. A similar relationship exists among people who combine for any kind of collective action—in commerce, in government, in every human enterprise.

And so, without analyzing in detail every section of the cone and every rank and position in any administrative or public enterprise from the lowest to the highest, we see a law by which people combine to take collective action in relationships such that the more directly they participate in carrying out the action, the less they can direct it, and the more they direct, the less they directly participate. The proportion rises from the soldiers at the base of the cone to its single apex—the supreme commander, who takes the least direct part in the action and devotes his activity primarily to commanding.
This relationship of the people who command to those who carry out the commands is what constitutes the essence of the concept called power.

Having restored the condition of time—under which all events occur—we find that a command is only carried out when it corresponds to an actual series of events. Restoring the essential condition of the relationship between those who command and those who execute, we find that by the very nature of the case, those who command take the least direct part in the event itself, and that their activity is devoted exclusively to commanding.
